domains.title: Chilsong, the Seven Stars
domains.subtitle: celestial spirits of the Big Dipper, longevity, and fate
domains.lead: Chilsong is the seven stars, spirits of the Big Dipper who govern longevity, fate, and protection from calamity in Korean tradition. The name means "Seven stars" and belongs to the domain "Seven Stars, Ursa Major." Chilsong means "seven stars" and refers especially to the seven stars of the Big Dipper (Ursa Major). In Korean religion the seven stars are worshipped as Chilseongsin, benevolent spirits who grant longevity, avert disaster, and guide the dead.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Chilsong is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Seven Spirits of the Dipper
myths.text: The seven stars are personified as seven spirits or seven buddhas who preside over human fate. Each star is associated with a particular blessing, such as longevity, wealth, or protection from illness.

myths.title: The Chilsong-jae
myths.text: Buddhist temples performed Chilsong-jae, rituals dedicated to the seven stars. The rite combined invocation of the Big Dipper with Confucian cosmological symbolism, seeking the welfare of the state and the people.

myths.title: Chilseong in the Gut
myths.text: In shamanic ritual, Chilseongsin is honoured as a merciful celestial figure. Shamans petition the seven stars to extend life, cure disease, and guide the spirits of the dead to a better realm.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 七 (chil, "seven") and 星 (song, "star"). Read 칠성 in Korean, it refers to the seven stars of the Big Dipper and the spirits associated with them.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Chilsong, the Hangul form is 칠성 and the Hanja form is 七星. Hangul ‘칠성’ and Hanja ‘七星’; the figure is also known as Chilseongsin in shamanic and Buddhist contexts. The ASCII form chilsong is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Chilsong is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Chilsong is a layered figure. Its astronomical core is shared across East Asia, but in Korea it was shaped by Buddhist star rituals, Daoist longevity practices, and shamanic invocation. Joseon court ritual honoured the seven stars for the welfare of the dynasty, while village practice sought protection for ordinary families. The figure also overlaps with Chinese Xuanwu (Dark Warrior) symbolism and with Buddhist representations of stellar buddhas. Despite these borrowings, the Korean Chilseong-gut has a distinctive musical and choreographic form.
lore.culturalLegacy: Chilsong remains visible in Korean temple art, shamanic paintings, and prayers for longevity. The seven-star motif decorates talismans, funeral garments, and ritual implements. In popular culture, the Big Dipper appears in Korean astronomy education, video games, and media about fate and destiny. The figure also informs Korean Buddhist identity, where Chilseong is one of the most commonly invoked protective deities.
lore.extendedMeditation: Chilsong invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
